market_context: United States/general English; USDA composition and carotenoid bioavailability
title: Raw vs. cooked tomato: what happens to lycopene?

seo.title: Raw vs. cooked tomato: lycopene and vitamins
seo.meta_description: Cooking tomato can lower vitamin C but break the plant matrix and make lycopene more bioavailable. Dietary fat also improves carotenoid absorption.
seo.search_intent: Understand why cooked tomato can improve lycopene availability despite losses of heat-sensitive vitamins.

excerpt: Cooking tomato does not create lycopene, but it can make the pigment more bioavailable by disrupting cell walls and changing its physical form. Vitamin C and other heat-sensitive compounds can decline at the same time. Eating tomato with some fat, such as olive oil, also supports absorption of fat-soluble carotenoids.
content_html:
Tomato shows why “raw keeps more nutrients” is too simple. Heat can reduce one nutrient while making another easier to absorb.

Lycopene is trapped in the plant matrix

Raw tomato holds carotenoids inside cell structures. Crushing and heating disrupt those structures and can shift lycopene into forms that are incorporated more readily into digestive micelles.

More per 100 grams can also mean less water

Tomato sauce and paste can look dramatically higher in lycopene because water has been removed. That is concentration, not lycopene being manufactured by heat. Bioavailability is a separate effect.

FeatureRaw tomatoCooked tomato
LycopenePresent in intact matrixOften more concentrated and accessible
Lycopene absorptionGenerally lowerCan improve
Vitamin CBetter retainedCan decline with heat/time
Water/textureHigh water, firmSofter, may be concentrated

Fat helps carotenoid absorption

Lycopene is fat-soluble. Tomato cooked or served with a modest amount of olive oil provides both a disrupted plant matrix and dietary fat for carotenoid absorption.

You do not have to pick one format

Raw tomato provides volume, freshness and vitamin C; cooked tomato makes lycopene more accessible. Both can belong in the same diet.

The takeaway

Cooking changes the tomato rather than simply improving or damaging it. For lycopene availability, cooking is often beneficial.

faq.question: Does cooked tomato contain more lycopene?
faq.answer: It may be more concentrated per 100 g when water is lost, but the key effect is improved bioavailability rather than heat creating lycopene.

faq.question: Does olive oil help?
faq.answer: Yes. Dietary fat helps absorb lycopene and other fat-soluble carotenoids.
